paper_title: Lang-SVG: Hierarchical Image Vectorization with Language Priors

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Image vectorization reconstructs raster images as compact scalable vector graph- ics (SVG), providing a structured and editable code representation of images. However, most existing vectorization methods optimize for pixel-level render- ing fidelity, often producing SVGs that lack alignment with human-perceived object-part hierarchies, making them difficult to manipulate. To address this, we propose Lang-SVG, which introduces an explicit tree structure to organize SVG primitives with semantic labels and parent-child relationships. Lang-SVG incorporates granularity-controllable and open-vocabulary segmentation priors to initialize object-part hierarchies and leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with SVG tree context to assign semantic labels to unlabeled nodes. To reduce redundancy, we introduce depth-adaptive simplification to reduce shape complexity and Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging to eliminate redundant SVG nodes. L1-SAM-Prompting further recovers missing regions to improve recon- struction fidelity and structural completeness. Beyond reconstruction fidelity, we introduce a new evaluation protocol that measures structural quality and semantic part alignment. Experiments demonstrate that Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art performance in both rendering fidelity and structural quality. Project website: https://xiliu8006.github.io/Lang-SVG/.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Image vectorization transforms raster images into compact scalable vector graphics (SVG), providing structured, renderable, and editable code representation of visual content. As text-based representation, SVG is increasingly becoming an interface between images and language models. Recent MLLMs learn to generate SVG code [14], benchmarks evaluate visual understanding through Corresponding author: Siyu Huang 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). image-to-SVG generation [5, 6], and code-based approaches [711] explore structured visual code for generation, manipulation, and reasoning. However, existing SVG datasets [1, 2, 12, 13] largely focus on icons and illustrations, offering limited coverage of complex natural images. Vectorizing natural images offers much larger and more diverse source of SVG code beyond simple icons and illustrations, but representing their complex visual content as structured code remains challenging. Recent differentiable SVG methods [1417] have substantially advanced image vectorization in terms of rendering fidelity, efficiency, and compactness, with recent approaches [1820, 4] further exploring layered and semantic representations to improve editability. However, these methods typically organize SVG primitives as flat layers without explicitly encoding object-part hierarchies. As result, primitives belonging to the same object may be distributed across different layers, making it difficult to select and edit individual objects or their parts. Moreover, without hierarchical guidance, SVG optimization may allocate excessive primitives to redundant shapes or high-frequency textures rather than meaningful semantic regions. These limitations highlight the need for image vectorization that preserves semantic structure while maintaining high rendering fidelity. We argue that this limitation partly stems from the lack of explicit semantic and structural constraints in existing image vectorization objectives. While pixel-level reconstruction losses effectively optimize SVG geometry, opacity, and color, they do not explicitly encourage primitives to form meaningful semantic structures. SGLIVE [19] incorporates SAM [21] to improve structural alignment, but SAM masks do not explicitly capture fine-grained semantic object-part hierarchies. LIVSS [18] further employs diffusion-based simplification to generate images at multiple semantic levels, followed by SAM to extract masks from coarse semantic level to fine-grained level. However, diffusion-based simplification may distort geometric details, causing shape boundaries to deviate from the image. To address these issues, we propose Lang-SVG, tree-structured SVG representation that organizes vector primitives with semantic labels and parent-child hierarchy, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Unlike flat SVG representations, our hierarchical structure explicitly models object-part relationships while preserving the flexibility of free-form vector primitives. We initialize its semantic hierarchy with openvocabulary segmentation [22] and enrich it with coarse-to-fine masks from granularity-controllable models such as Semantic-SAM [23], avoiding the geometric distortions introduced by diffusion-based simplification. However, these masks often contain overlapping or redundant regions, making direct vectorization difficult under limited control-point budget. We therefore introduce depth-adaptive simplification to allocate geometric complexity according to tree depth, and Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging module to remove redundant regions while preserving semantically labeled nodes. We further introduce L1-SAM-Prompting, which uses reconstruction residuals to prompt SAM for coherent missing regions, progressively refining the tree beyond the initial segmentation masks. Our experiments demonstrate that the explicit tree structure improves both reconstruction fidelity and alignment with human-perceived image structures. Beyond hierarchical image vectorization, Lang-SVG further supports SVG semantic labeling. While open-vocabulary segmentation provides initial semantic labels, finer regions introduced during tree refinement may remain unlabeled. To address this, we develop tree-guided semantic tagging method that leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with visual evidence and hierarchical SVG context, including parent, sibling, and child relationships. This enables semantic labeling beyond the initial segmentation models, supporting semantic selection and part-level manipulation. Evaluating hierarchical SVG vectorization requires going beyond photometric and perceptual metrics, which cannot determine whether SVG primitives align with human-perceived object-part structures. We therefore introduce new evaluation protocol that combines StructXLIP [24], structure-aware vision-language model for measuring image-level structural similarity, with part/subpart recall to assess the alignment between SVG regions and human annotations at different IoU thresholds. On the ADE20K [25] dataset, Lang-SVG improves StructXLIP from 0.462 to 0.506 and average part recall from 28.8% to 48.5% at 576 control points, while achieving the best reconstruction performance among the compared methods. Furthermore, incorporating SVG tree context improves semantic tagging accuracy from 58.5% to 81.3% in our masked-label evaluation, demonstrating the value of hierarchical information for semantic reasoning. Overall, our contributions are summarized as follows: To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to construct hierarchical SVG trees with semantic labeling from raster images. 2 We propose Lang-SVG, novel hierarchical SVG representation with semantic labels and parent-child relationships. To handle the complex and redundant masks introduced by Semantic-SAMs fine-grained, multi-level segmentation, we introduce depth-adaptive simplification and tree-guided pruning and merging. We further introduce L1-SAM-Prompting to recover missing regions and tree-aware MLLM labeling for semantic tagging. We propose new evaluation protocol for image vectorization that goes beyond reconstruction fidelity by measuring structural quality and semantic part alignment. The experiments show that Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art results under both reconstruction fidelity and structural quality.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Image vectorization. Image vectorization transforms raster image into parametric representation, enabling resolution-independent rendering while making the image directly editable by humans [2630]. DiffVG [14] was among the first works to make the rendering of SVG differentiable, reformulating the vectorization task as an end-to-end optimization problem. Bézier Splatting [15] improves rendering efficiency by introducing splatting-based formulation inspired by 2D Gaussian representations [31], making vectorization more practical for high-resolution rendering. LIVE [20] introduces layer-wise coarse-to-fine strategy that progressively adds primitives, improving the quality and topology of SVG representations. Subsequent works [17, 16] address the over-complexity of SVGs by simplifying vector representations and applying add-and-prune strategies to remove redundant primitives. Beyond compactness, SGLIVE [19], LIVSS [18] and SemLayer [32] incorporate segmentation priors to better align vectorized shapes with the structural information underlying natural image textures, leading to more semantically meaningful decompositions. AmodalSVG [33] goes further by peeling semantically complete raster layers with MLLM guidance and inpainting. recent line of work reformulates vectorization as an SVG code generation task with MLLMs. StarVector [1], OmniSVG [2], InternSVG [34] and IR4RL [10] perform image-to-SVG generation directly in the SVG code space, leveraging semantic visual understanding to predict richer primitives and more compact outputs. These methods indicate that vectorization is moving from pure reconstruction toward editability and semantic decomposition. However, most existing methods still represent SVGs as an ordered set of primitives, or first separate semantic regions in the raster domain and then vectorize them independently. In contrast, our proposed Lang-SVG representation explicitly encodes parent-child relations and semantics among SVG nodes, enabling applications such as grouping and semantic analysis of SVG primitives. Open-vocabulary segmentation. Open-vocabulary segmentation provides flexible way to extract semantic regions from images using language-level concepts, which is particularly useful for semantic vectorization. The SAM family [21, 35, 36] has enabled general-purpose promptable mask generation across diverse image domains, with recent variants further extending prompts from points and boxes to concept-level inputs. However, these semantic prompts are typically provided by users. Grounded SAM [22] addresses this limitation by coupling open-vocabulary detection or tagging with SAM-based segmentation: semantic candidates are first localized or generated automatically, and SAM is then applied to produce the corresponding masks. In this way, language-level concepts can be converted into raster-domain candidate masks with less manual prompting, providing useful guidance for downstream vectorization. Some works [37, 38] further target open-vocabulary part segmentation and object-part parsing. Another line of work [23, 39, 40] improves the granularity and semantic controllability of segmentation foundation models, enabling finer-grained masks. Our work leverages open-vocabulary segmentation and granularity-controllable SAM models to introduce semantically aligned hierarchical information into image vectorization. This hierarchical structure allows vectorized layers to better align with object-part semantics, and further supports tagging semantically meaningful regions that are not explicitly parsed by the segmentation model. Multimodal large language model. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are typically pretrained via next-token prediction over heterogeneous inputs, including images, text, and videos. Early MLLMs, such as BLIP [41], Flamingo [42], and Idefics [43], introduce cross-attention mechanisms to facilitate interaction between visual and linguistic representations. Modern MLLMs largely follow the paradigm popularized by LLaVA [44], where visual tokens produced by pretrained vision encoders such as CLIP [45] are projected into the LLM backbone. This design simplifies multimodal 3 Figure 2: Overview of Lang-SVG framework. Given an input image, we initialize hierarchical Lang-SVG tree from multi-granularity and open-vocabulary segmentation masks. The tree is iteratively refined through differentiable SVG optimization, L1-SAM-Prompting to recover missing regions, and Add & Prune operations to add new leaves and prune redundant ones. fusion while retaining strong language modeling capabilities. Recent research shows that MLLMs can ground language in visual content, leveraging both visual and text context with implicit commonsense knowledge acquired during large-scale training [4650]. We utilize MLLMs to predict unknown tags of SVG representations conditioned on visual inputs and structured semantic context derived from tree-based representation.

sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.content: Given an input raster image RHW 3, we aim to construct tree-structured SVG representation that achieves high-fidelity rendering while preserving the semantic hierarchy and fine-grained structural details of the original image. We define = (V, E, r), vk = (yk, sk, mk). (1) Here, = {vk}K k=1 is the set of nodes, defines the parentchild relationships, and is the root node. Each edge (vk, vk) indicates that vk is semantic constituent of vk. Each node vk stores semantic tag yk, semantic mask mk, and set of SVG primitives parameterized by sk. 3.1 SVG Tree Construction via Granularity-Controllable Segmentation To construct tree-structured SVG representation that preserves semantic hierarchies and fine-grained structural details, we first obtain masks with semantic tags from open-vocabulary [22] or subpartaware segmentation methods [38, 37], as shown in Fig. 2. These masks initialize semantic tree with labeled object-part regions. We then enrich the tree with multi-granularity masks from granularitycontrollable segmentation models, such as Semantic-SAM [23] and UnSAM [39]. These additional masks are initially assigned unknown semantic tags and serve as candidate nodes for refining the hierarchy. Formally, the multi-granularity masks are defined as {M(ℓ)}L ℓ=1, M(ℓ) = {m(ℓ) }, (2) where each set M(ℓ) contains masks at specific semantic granularity. We construct the hierarchy by inserting candidate masks from coarse to fine based on spatial containment. node vk is considered candidate parent of vk if mk mk mk τ. (3) Among valid parents, we select the node at the greatest tree depth, breaking ties by mask IoU. If no valid parent exists, the node is attached to the full-image root. This process organizes segmentation masks into explicit parent-child relationships rather than flat layers, providing hierarchical structure for subsequent SVG initialization and optimization. Appendix A.2 provides the complete construction and update procedures. 3.2 Tree-Guided SVG Optimization Tree-guided SVG initialization. For each node vk, we convert its mask mk into polygon, which is then approximated by set of Bézier curves to initialize the corresponding vector layer Lk as closed region. key challenge arises during this conversion: masks from coarser segmentation levels tend to have complex, irregular boundaries, yet due to alpha compositing, nodes closer to the tree root are more occluded and contribute less to the final rendered image. Fitting all masks with high-complexity polygons therefore introduces redundant primitives with little gain in reconstruction quality. To address this, we propose depth-adaptive simplification. Rather than using fixed tolerance for all nodes, we adapt the approximation tolerance according to the nodes depth in the tree: nodes closer to the root are fitted with higher tolerance, yielding simpler polygons, while leaf nodes use lower tolerance to preserve fine-grained boundary details. This allocates geometric complexity in proportion to visual contribution, achieving better balance between reconstruction fidelity and primitive efficiency. L1-SAM-Prompting. common practice in image vectorization is to initialize SVG primitives from clusters derived from the L1 loss map between the current rendering and the target image. While this improves reconstruction metrics such as PSNR, it tends to allocate primitives toward fitting high-frequency textures rather than capturing structurally meaningful regions, resulting in insufficient representation of semantic structure. Although LIVSS [18] incorporates SAM to generate masks, it still relies on loss-driven clustering to meet path budgets and improve visual quality, since even with dense point prompts, SAM is not intended to produce fine-grained masks. To address this, we propose L1-SAM-Prompting, which bridges loss-driven mask generation and SAM. Instead of directly using L1 clustering masks for SVG initialization, we extract their bounding boxes and mean points as prompts for SAM, producing masks that are more coherent and structurally complete, rather than dominated by frequency discrepancies between low-frequency SVG renderings and high-frequency natural images. We integrate this strategy as an intermediate step between two optimization stages: structure optimization stage that fits segmentation-derived masks, and visual refinement stage that refines appearance details. The L1-SAM-Prompting step generates supplementary masks that emphasize meaningful structures rather than noise from pixel-level loss, improving the balance between structural representation and visual fidelity. Tree-guided pruning and merging. Multi-granularity segmentation produces large number of masks that are often redundant and unstable. common approach is to prune masks based on spatial overlap (e.g., IoU); however, IoU-based pruning is insufficient, as it fails to remove masks with different shapes but similar appearance and semantics. Rather than relying solely on geometric overlap, our representation enables appearance-aware pruning using the associated SVG layers. Specifically, we compare each node with its parent based on the color of their SVG layers: if an unlabeled child node exhibits high color similarity to its parent, we remove it; parentchild or sibling nodes within the same semantic branch can be merged when they exhibit similar color and sufficient spatial overlap. These branch constraints prevent similarly colored regions from different objects from being merged. Color and overlap therefore identify rendering redundancy within branch rather than establish semantic identity. Nodes that already carry semantic tags are preserved and excluded from pruning or merging to retain semantic information. 3.3 Tree-Guided Semantic Labeling with Multimodal Large Language Models Given tree-structured SVG representation , our objective is to assign semantic labels to nodes with unknown tags. We focus on unlabeled nodes within subtrees rooted at semantically labeled nodes, allowing us to exploit hierarchical context. As shown in Fig. 4, we use Qwen3.5-27B [51] to predict the semantic label of each unlabeled node by jointly considering its local neighborhood and ancestral context within the tree. For each unlabeled node vk, we construct structured prompt containing the full image, crop extracted from the bounding box of the target SVG region, and its RGB color from SVG primitives. We further include parent and ancestor tags to define the semantic scope, along with labeled sibling and child tags and sibling bounding boxes to provide local relational and spatial cues for disambiguation. The prompt is formulated as structured decision task, where the MLLM is asked to infer the semantic tag of the target node based on these visual and hierarchical cues. We consider both closed-set and 5 open-vocabulary settings. In the closed-set setting, the MLLM selects label from predefined candidate set, while in the open-vocabulary setting, it predicts free-form tag. Ambiguous nodes are assigned default texture or unknown tag to avoid unreliable semantic over-assignment. This process augments the SVG tree with node-level semantic labels, enabling vector primitives to be organized by both geometry and semantic identity. Table 5 shows that the tree structure provides useful context for semantic tag recovery.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experiment Setup Datasets. Existing image vectorization methods [20, 19], support only reconstruction metrics and provide neither multi-level object-part hierarchies nor node-level semantic labels. Therefore, we therefore conduct our main evaluation on ADE20K-Part234 [25], whose diverse natural scenes are annotated with object, part, and subpart masks and labels. These annotations allow us to test whether SVG regions align with human-annotated parts, whether parent-child relations and semantic tags are correct, and whether tree context helps recover missing tags. We uniformly sample 200 validation images, which contain 752 ground-truth part/subpart masks. To test generalization, we further use COCO-AOKVQA [52], whose image descriptions enable text-to-image semantic evaluation, and 40 complex SVG-style images selected from Iconfont [13]. Evaluation metrics. We first evaluate reconstruction fidelity using SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, and CLIP similarity. However, these metrics do not fully capture the structural details of an image or its semantic object-part hierarchy. Therefore, we adopt StructXLIP [24], structure-aware vision-language model trained with edge-based cues, to measure image-level structural similarity, and introduce part/subpart recall on ADE20K-Part234 to evaluate the alignment between SVG regions and ground-truth parts and subparts at different IoU thresholds. To evaluate semantic alignment, we compute text-to-image (t2i) CLIP and StructXLIP similarities between COCO-AOKVQA image descriptions and rendered SVGs. To evaluate the correctness of SVG semantic hierarchies, we introduce three additional metrics: Child Containment measures the fraction of an SVG childs area covered by its ground-truth parent; Tagging Reliability measures the fraction of labeled SVG region covered by the ground-truth subpart with the same label; and Labeled Subpart Recall measures the fraction of ground-truth subparts recovered by SVG children with the correct parent, label, and IoU above given threshold. All three metrics are reported at thresholds of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. Evaluation mode. Since different vectorization methods use different SVG parameterizations, fair comparison should control the total number of points. LIVE [20] and DiffVG [14] use fixed representation, so the number of paths directly determines the total point budget. In contrast, LIVSS [18] and our method convert masks to SVG paths, and each path may contain different number of points. Therefore, we report two protocols. Same points is our main protocol, where all methods are compared under the same total number of points. We also report Same paths for LIVSS [18] and our method, using the same number of SVG paths to ensure fair comparison. 4.2 Comparison to Baselines Quantitative and Qualitative results. We compare Lang-SVG with state-of-the-art differentiable SVG vectorization methods, including SGLIVE [19] and LIVSS [18], which also leverage segmentation priors. As shown in Tables 1 and 2, our method consistently outperforms existing methods in both reconstruction fidelity and structural quality across all point budgets. At 576 control points, Lang-SVG improves StructXLIP from the second-best 0.462 to 0.506, and average part recall from 28.8 to 48.5. The improvements also hold under the Same paths protocol. As shown in Fig. 3, our method better preserves coherent object regions and fine-grained structures, especially under limited primitive budgets, rather than fitting local textures or reconstruction residuals. Starting from ADE20K groundtruth masks and labels, we construct SVG trees following Sec. 3.1 and randomly hide up to 50% of the part and subpart tags in each scene, while preserving the masks, node locations, and tree topology. The hidden tags are used only for evaluation. Given the full image, target region, and different subsets of tree context, Qwen3.5-27B predicts the missing tags from the closed ADE20K label set. This setup isolates semantic tagging from segmentation quality and evaluates the contribution of hierarchical context to label recovery. Table 5 shows that hierarchical context substantially improves tag prediction for subpart nodes. Visual evidence alone achieves 58.5% exact accuracy, which increases to 67.7% with object and parent identity and 68.9% with additional sibling and child labels. Including the geometric layout of parent, sibling, and child regions further improves accuracy to 80.2%, while adding region color statistics raises it to 81.3%. We further examine the contribution of visual inputs in A5 and A6 by removing localized crops or all image inputs. Even without these inputs, the structured context achieves accuracy close to the visual-only baseline, suggesting that the SVG tree itself provides substantial semantic information. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of hierarchical SVG context for node-level semantic tag recovery. We further evaluate the full pipeline without ground-truth masks or labels. In this setting, Lang-SVG is initialized using open-vocabulary part segmentation [38], followed by tree-guided semantic tagging of unlabeled SVG nodes. Ambiguous nodes can be assigned texture or unknown tags to avoid unreliable semantic predictions. 4.5 Ablation Study We conduct three ablation studies on ADE20K [25] under the 2304-point parameter budget to examine segmentation-prior replacement, tree-related designs, and the remaining modules. Segmentation priors and vectorization design. Table 6 compares segmentation-prior replacement in LIVSS with our complete vectorization framework. Replacing SAM with Semantic-SAM and Grounded-SAM in the LIVSS pipeline increases PSNR from 24.12 to 24.23 and StructXLIP from 0.6950 to 0.7081. Using the same segmentation priors, Lang-SVG further improves PSNR to 25.90 and StructXLIP to 0.775. Tree-guided pruning and merging operate on parentchild and sibling relations in the SVG tree and therefore require the tree structure; disabling the tree necessarily disables tree pruning. Finally, enabling pruning and merging in the w/o Tree Prune configuration improves PSNR from 25.71 to 25.90 and StructXLIP from 0.7687 to 0.775. This indicates that redundant masks otherwise remain and compete for the same parameter budget. L1-SAM-Prompting and segmentation backbone. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We present Lang-SVG, tree-structured SVG representation for hierarchical image vectorization and semantic labeling. Lang-SVG organizes SVG primitives into semantic object-part hierarchies and incorporates depth-adaptive simplification, Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging, and L1-SAMPrompting to reduce redundancy, recover missing regions, and improve rendering fidelity. We further introduce tree-guided semantic tagging method that leverages hierarchical context to guide MLLMs in labeling SVG nodes. To evaluate these representations beyond reconstruction fidelity, we propose new evaluation protocol that measures structural quality and semantic alignment. Experiments on ADE20K demonstrate that Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art performance in both rendering fidelity and structural quality, providing structured and semantically labeled SVG representations for editing and downstream tasks. Limitations and Future Work. Our method relies on open-vocabulary segmentation models to provide initial labels and language labels, such that the parsing quality is still partially bounded by the accuracy and granularity of these upstream models [54]. Missing parts, ambiguous masks, or incomplete labels may be inherited by the SVG tree, especially for small subparts and texturelike regions. Although our tree-guided MLLM assignment can recover many unknown tags using structural context, it is not yet specifically trained for SVG semantic understanding. promising future direction is to fine-tune MLLMs for SVG-aware labeling. By training on SVG trees, rendered vector regions, parent-child relations, and part-level annotations, such models could assign more accurate semantic tags to vector components, reduce dependence on open-vocabulary segmentation, and improve fine-grained parsing of complex natural images.

sections.title: A Appendix
sections.content: This appendix provides an additional evaluation on SVG-style images, the hierarchical SVG construction algorithms, the ADE20K tagging system prompt, and further qualitative vectorization and semantic-tagging results. A.1 Generalization to SVG-Style Images We evaluate 40 complex SVG-style images selected from Iconfont to complement the natural-image benchmarks. All methods use the same budget of 576 control points. Table 9 shows that LangSVG achieves the highest PSNR, SSIM, and CLIP similarity and the lowest LPIPS. Compared with the strongest PSNR baseline, SGLIVE, PSNR increases from 28.62 to 29.28. LIVE achieves the highest StructXLIP score, while our method scores 0.9549. These results demonstrate that the pipeline also applies to SVG-style content. This experiment measures reconstruction and perceptual quality; hierarchy and semantic-label quality are evaluated separately using ADE20K objectpart annotations in Sec. 4.3. Table 9: Vectorization of 40 complex SVG-style images selected from Iconfont [13] under the same 576-point budget. Best results are bold. We compare SVGs produced by DiffVG [14], LIVE [20], SGLIVE [19], LIVSS [18], and our method. A.2 Algorithms for Hierarchical SVG Construction Algorithms 1 and 2 detail the overall pipeline and the tree update procedure. Open-vocabulary masks initialize labeled semantic branches, while multi-granularity masks and reconstruction-driven 15 proposals add finer nodes. For each new mask, candidate parents are selected by spatial containment; the deepest candidate is preferred, with IoU used to break ties. The full-image root provides fallback. This geometric assignment rule supports masks at different granularities, although imperfect segmentation and partially overlapping regions can still produce ambiguous relations. The hierarchy evaluation in Sec. 4.3 measures the resulting parent alignment and label consistency. The complete set of 234 candidate labels is supplied as candidate_labels in the user message. Only the final JSON output schema is omitted from this display. You are an ADE20KPart234 scene-graph part classification evaluator. You will receive: - the original full image - crop around the containing object, when available - crop around the target bbox, when available - metadata copied from layered scene-graph JSON - known object/part context and sibling layout from that JSON - bbox layout metadata for the target, parent, siblings, and parent children - closed candidate list of valid part/subpart labels The ground-truth target node tag has been hidden. Classify the semantic part or subpart inside the target bbox using the image and the unmasked scene-graph context. Rules: - Choose exactly one label from candidate_labels. - Use the target bbox metadata to locate the masked part/subpart inside the full image and object crop. - Use the object crop for object-level context, not as the target region itself. - Use the target bbox crop for local visual details. - Use ancestor_tags, parent_tag, sibling_tags, child_tags, parent_layout, sibling_bboxes, and parent_child_layout from the JSON as context. - candidate_labels are the only valid outputs. They are full hierarchical labels; reason about their leaf part names, but output the exact candidate label string. - predicted_label must exactly match one candidate label string. - Do not invent new label outside the candidate list. - Return exactly one JSON object. - Do not output prose, markdown, or reasoning text. Before choosing the label, silently run this parent-to-subpart checklist: 1. Identify the parent object/part from ancestor_tags, parent_tag, and parent_layout. 2. Generate plausible child parts for that parent, then eliminate candidates whose position, size, color/material, or sibling layout is inconsistent. 3. Compare the target bbox with every sibling bbox under the same parent. Existing known siblings are strong constraints; masked siblings may still provide layout evidence through their bbox and color but not their hidden tag. 4. Use bbox_average_rgb and visual color/material continuity as supporting evidence. Similar color/texture can indicate another segment of the same object; very different color may indicate clothing, shoe, material detail, or texture. 5. Avoid impossible duplicate anatomy or object parts unless the image and layout clearly support duplication. Choose "unknown" only if no candidate label is spatially and visually plausible, but prefer valid candidate when evidence is sufficient. Examples of the intended reasoning: - If parent is person and known siblings already include left/right arm, third arm candidate at the lower body is usually wrong; lower bbox near feet is more likely leg, foot, shoe, or clothing depending on shape and color. - If parent is persons leg and the target bbox is at the bottom end with shoe-like color/shape, prefer the candidate whose leaf is foot or shoe over hand or arm. - If parent is persons face/head, small upper symmetric boxes are likely eyes; central box below eyes and above mouth is likely nose; lower face box is more likely mouth/chin than eye. - If parent is car/vehicle, lower left/right boxes are likely wheel/tire; boxes in the upper body are more likely window, door, mirror, or light. - If one known sibling is wheel on the lower left and the target is similar colored/size lower-right box, the target is likely another wheel candidate. 17 A.4 Additional Qualitative Results We compare the SVG outputs generated by DiffVG [14], LIVE [20], LIVSS [18], and our method under the same point-budget setting. These examples show that Lang-SVG better preserves the visual structure of natural images while maintaining high rendering fidelity. We also include more semantic SVG tagging examples, where our tree-guided semantic assignment predicts meaningful object, part, and subpart labels for SVG components. Figure 6: More comparison results. We compare SVGs produced by DiffVG [14], LIVE [20], LIVSS [18], and our method. Our SVGs better align with the target images and preserve more coherent visual structures. Figure 7: More comparison results under lower point budget. We compare SVGs produced by DiffVG [14], LIVE [20], LIVSS [18], and our method. Our method produces SVGs with better visual fidelity and more coherent structure under the same point budget. Figure 8: More semantic SVG tagging results. We show additional examples of semantic tags predicted for SVG components using our tree-guided semantic assignment.
